Exercise 1 — Basic Maps and Graphs in R

BSTA 374 · 12 points · Due Thursday, September 10, 2026, 11:59 pm

Authors

Eric M. Delmelle · Lehigh University

Student: Maggie Sobaszek

Published

September 16, 2026

What this exercise is

Your first graded work in this course. It covers the first two weeks: reading spatial data with sf, understanding what a coordinate reference system is and moving between them, and producing honest choropleth and point maps with both ggplot2 and tmap.

No data to download. Everything runs on the North Carolina SIDS data that ships inside the sf package, so your analysis will reproduce on my machine exactly as it does on yours — which is the point.

Each part ends with starting code. Copy it, fill in the blanks marked ______, and adapt it. It is scaffolding, not a solution: the mechanical lines are given so that your time goes into the parts that require judgement.

Part A — Read and describe the data (2 points)

Answer each in one or two sentences of prose, outside the code chunks, and show the code you used to find out.

  1. How many features does nc contain, and what does one row represent?

The feature ‘nc’ contains 100 features. One row represents a county

  1. What geometry type is stored? Why is it that type rather than POLYGON?

Multipolygon is the geometry type. It is used because places on the coast have counties that include islands, which are separate polygons. All geometry types need to be the same in R, so all geometry types are multipolygons.

  1. What coordinate reference system is the data in? Give its name, say whether it is geographic or projected, and say how you found out.

The coordinate reference system is NAD27 and is geographic. I found it at the top with “Geodetic CRS: NAD27” Then I found the type with st_is_longlat(nc) = TRUE, which is geographic.

  1. In your own words, what do BIR74 and SID74 measure? Why does having both matter more than having either one alone?

BIR74 measures births from 1974 to 1978 in NC and SID74 measures sudden infant deaths in NC from the same time period. Having both available means you can calculate rates and ratios, which allows for better comparison between counties.

Part B — Coordinate reference systems (2 points)

  1. Transform nc to EPSG:32119 (NAD83 / North Carolina State Plane, in metres) and store it as a new object. Do not overwrite nc — you need both.
  2. Plot the counties before and after, near enough to each other that a reader can compare them. One or two sentences on what visibly changed.

In the maps, p1 is curved downward more on the western side of NC compared to p2.

  1. Compute the area of every county in square kilometres, using the projected version. Report the five largest.

The five largest are Columbus, Robeson, Sampson, Bladen, and Wake.

  1. Now compute areas from the unprojected object as well. Compare the two sets of numbers and explain, in two or three sentences, what sf did and why the projected version is the one you would report in a paper.

When calculating area on the unprojected data (nc), sf treated the Earth as a curved 3D globe, using degrees. When using the projected data (nc_proj), it measured area on a flat 2D map, using meters.
I would use the projected version. Using that gives exact, standardized measurements in units we regularly use to calculate distance (meters/kilometers) and is easier for people to understand.

Note

Step 4 will not give you an error, and the two sets of numbers will be close but not identical. That is the interesting part — the question is which surface each answer refers to.

Starting code

# B1
nc_proj <- st_transform(nc, 32119)

# B2 -- one plot each
p1 <- ggplot(nc)      + geom_sf(fill = "grey90", colour = "white") + theme_void()
p2 <- ggplot(nc_proj) + geom_sf(fill = "grey90", colour = "white") + theme_void()

p1
p2
p1+p2
# side by side, if you like:  library(patchwork);  p1 + p2

# B3 -- st_area() returns square METRES, as a units object
nc_proj <- nc_proj |>
  mutate(area_km2 = as.numeric(units::set_units(st_area(nc_proj), km^2)))

nc_proj |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  slice_max(area_km2, n = 5) |>
  select(NAME, area_km2)
      NAME area_km2
1 Columbus 2450.349
2  Robeson 2439.238
3  Sampson 2437.410
4   Bladen 2288.424
5     Wake 2194.261
# B4 -- now do the same starting from nc (degrees) and compare
nc <- nc |>
  mutate(area_km2 = as.numeric(units::set_units(st_area(nc), km^2)))

nc |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  slice_max(area_km2, n = 5) |>
  select(NAME, area_km2)
      NAME area_km2
1 Columbus 2450.831
2  Robeson 2439.935

Part C — Choropleth maps (5 points)

This is the largest part of the exercise, and it is as much about judgement as about code.

  1. Add a column giving the SIDS rate per 1,000 live births for 1974–78.
  2. Make a choropleth of the raw counts (SID74) and one of the rate, using ggplot2. Then write three or four sentences explaining why the two maps disagree, and which one you would put in front of a health department, and why.

The first one shows the total count of SIDS in a county and the second one shows the rate of SIDS per 1,000 live births. In the one that shows only the count, there is nothing to compare it to, so while some counties seem high and others don’t, it’s hard to understand how serious it is. I would use the map that shows the rate, which highlights different counties and shows the number of SIDS compared to the number of births, which helps to give perspective.

  1. Rebuild the rate map using tmap. Same information, other package.

  2. Vary the class intervals on the rate map: produce it at least three ways — for instance equal intervals, quantiles, and Jenks natural breaks. Two or three sentences on how much the apparent geography of risk changes. Name the classification you would defend, and say why.

In some maps, like the ones using equal or pretty, seem to minimize the risks, where most regions appear lighter colored, having lower SIDS rates. Using quantiles, the risks seem higher, with more counties appearing darker colored. I would defend using Jenks natural breaks because it takes into account and breaks apart groups with trying to minimize the variance in groups.

  1. Every map you submit must have a legend with units, a title, thin boundaries that do not overwhelm the fill, and a perceptually uniform, colour-blind-safe palette. State in one sentence which palette you chose and why, including whether dark means high or low.

I chose the YlOrRd palette, where dark means high, because with red being a color that is associated with danger and not often used for positive indicators, is a good color choice for SIDS rates.

TipWhat earns full marks here

Not the prettiest map — the map whose choices you can defend. A student who picks quantiles and explains the trade-off in two clear sentences scores higher than one who picks Jenks because it looked nicer.

Starting code

# C1 -- deaths per 1,000 live births
nc <- nc |>
  mutate(rate74 = 1000 * SID74 / BIR74)

# C2 -- counts, then rates. Same code, one variable changed.
ggplot(nc) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = SID74), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.15) +
  scale_fill_distiller(palette = "Reds", direction = 1) +
  labs(title = "Sudden infant death count, 1974-78") +
  theme_void()
ggplot(nc) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = rate74), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.15) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "cividis", direction = -1, name = "per 1,000") +
  labs(title = "Sudden infant death rate, 1974-78") +
  theme_void()
# other palettes to try:
#   scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "viridis" / "plasma" / "cividis" / "mako")
#   scale_fill_distiller(palette = "YlOrRd", direction = 1)
#   RColorBrewer::display.brewer.all()   # shows every ColorBrewer option

# C3 -- the same map in tmap
tmap_mode("plot")                        # "view" makes it interactive
ℹ tmap modes "plot" - "view"
ℹ toggle with `tmap::ttm()`
tm_shape(nc) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "rate74") +
  tm_title("Sudden infant death rate, 1974-78")
# C4 -- change ONLY the classification, so the comparison is fair
tm_shape(nc) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "rate74",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile", n = 5, values = "brewer.YlOrRd"),
    fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "SIDS per 1,000 births"),
    #    fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "SIDS per 1,000 births", frame = FALSE),
    col = "black", lwd = 0.3) +
  tm_title("Quantiles") +
  tm_layout(frame = FALSE)

WarningA note on tmap versions

tmap changed its argument names in version 4. If an example you find online uses tm_polygons(col = ...) or style = ... directly and yours errors, check packageVersion("tmap") and read the help page rather than guessing. The code above is written for version 4.

Part D — A point layer (2 points)

  1. Look up the approximate longitude and latitude of four cities in North Carolina and build a small table holding the name and the two coordinates. Cite where you got the coordinates.
  2. Turn that table into an sf object with the correct CRS. State which EPSG code you used and why.

I used 4326 because we’re using longitude and latitude to define locations and this code uses degrees whereas projected uses meters.

  1. Plot the four cities on top of your rate choropleth, labelled legibly.
  2. One sentence: what would go wrong if you built the sf object with the coordinate columns in the other order?

The points would not be in North Carolina because longitude and latitude are switched, they would be somewhere on the opposite side in the southern part of the globe.

Starting code

# D1 -- North Carolina longitudes are NEGATIVE (west of Greenwich)
cities <- tibble(
  name = c("Cleveland", "Davidson", "Southport", "Asheville"),
  lon  = c(-80.67701, -80.83912, -78.01933, -82.55402),
  lat  = c(35.7332, 35.50233, 33.91821, 35.60095)
)

# D2 -- coords takes the column names in x, y order: longitude FIRST
cities_sf <- cities |>
  st_as_sf(coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326)

# D3 -- layers draw in order, so points come after polygons
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = nc, aes(fill = rate74), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.15) +
  geom_sf(data = cities_sf, size = 1.5, colour = "black") +
  geom_sf_text(data = cities_sf, aes(label = name), size = 3, nudge_y = 0.12) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "magma", direction = -1, name = "per 1,000") +
  theme_void()
Warning in st_point_on_surface.sfc(sf::st_zm(x)): st_point_on_surface may not
give correct results for longitude/latitude data
# check your cities landed in North Carolina and not in the ocean

Writing counts for roughly 10% of the mark within each part: the prose should be in complete sentences and free of obvious errors. Every part asks for interpretation as well as code — a submission that is all code and no sentences cannot score above about 60%.

Getting help

  • Office hours, or email me — with the code and the exact error message, not a screenshot of the whole console.
  • The sf documentation is genuinely good: vignette("sf1", package = "sf").
  • Moraga Chapter 2 covers most of Parts A–C.
  • If you are stuck for more than about thirty minutes on something that feels mechanical, that is a signal to ask rather than to persevere.
